title: Forgiveness close
hook: sixty days on the hardest gift

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was different answers: return, grace, mercy, release, reciprocity. Your line was kept whole, in its own words.

A brother runs down a road toward the twin who cheated him. Genesis says it plainly, in the King James words: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." That was early in this block. Since then: a guard who reached out his hand, a bedtime prayer, a Jain phrase sent wide, a day of fasting, and a long list of people who are hard to forgive. Sixty days on what this path called the hardest gift. Today it all gathers up, and then comes the one thing the whole block has been circling: let one thing go.
screen: `ESAU RUNS.` → `SIXTY DAYS ON THE HARDEST GIFT.` → `LET ONE THING GO.`

segments.voice: First, what forgiveness isn't. Forgiving is not excusing: the wrong stays named as a wrong. It isn't the same as reconciling, which takes two people and happens only where it's safe. And not yet is allowed. Second, the order. A Jewish teaching said that for wrongs between people, you go to the person first. Jesus told the one bringing a gift to leave it at the altar and be reconciled first. A good apology owns the wrong and repairs it. Third, the stories. Joseph wept aloud before his brothers. Esau ran. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at Ta'if, did not curse the town that drove him out. Angulimala stopped. Each is a picture of something held, and a hand that opens. Fourth, the times set aside: the Days of Awe and Yom Kippur, Kshamavani, Forgiveness Sunday, the Night of Power, the small nightly prayer before sleep, and yesterday's five answers, each in its own home. So what does let it go mean, after all that? Not that the thing was fine. Not forgetting, or going back. It means you stop carrying it everywhere you go. Paul's letter to the Colossians puts it in the King James words: "forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any". A quarrel is real. And it can still be set down.
screen: `NOT EXCUSING. NOT ALWAYS RETURNING.` · `THE PERSON FIRST.` · `A HAND THAT OPENS.` · `THE TIMES SET ASIDE.` · then, large: `LET IT GO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing you've been carrying, a comment, a slight, a grudge with no one left to argue with, and name it silently as what it was. Rest one hand palm up on your knee as if it sat there, and on each slow out-breath let the hand soften: not saying it was okay, just putting it down for now. If it comes back, notice it and set it down again; if you pray, you can offer it in your own way.
Quarrel. Paul's word in Colossians for the real complaint that forbearing and forgiving can still set down. Today's word.
Your line: let it go. Sixty days on the hardest gift, gathered into three words. Tomorrow, a new question: awe.

howItsDone: Some traditions mark forgiveness with a gesture of release, such as casting crumbs into water at Tashlich, asking forgiveness aloud at Kshamavani, or a bedtime prayer that forgives the day.
